title: The Outsiders | William Thorndike | Talks at Google
description:
What makes a successful CEO? Most people call to mind a familiar definition: “a seasoned manager with deep industry expertise.” Others might point to the qualities of today’s so-called celebrity CEOs—charisma, virtuoso communication skills, and a confident management style. But what really matters when you run an organization? What is the hallmark of exceptional CEO performance? Quite simply, it is the returns for the shareholders of that company over the long term.

In this refreshing, counterintuitive book, author Will Thorndike brings to bear the analytical wisdom of a successful career in investing, closely evaluating the performance of companies and their leaders. You will meet eight individualistic CEOs whose firms’ average returns outperformed the S&P 500 by a factor of twenty—in other words, an investment of $10,000 with each of these CEOs, on average, would have been worth over $1.5 million twenty-five years later. You may not know all their names, but you will recognize their companies: General Cinema, Ralston Purina, The Washington Post Company, Berkshire Hathaway, General Dynamics, Capital Cities Broadcasting, TCI, and Teledyne. In The Outsiders, you’ll learn the traits and methods—striking for their consistency and relentless rationality—that helped these unique leaders achieve such exceptional performance.

Humble, unassuming, and often frugal, these “outsiders” shunned Wall Street and the press, and shied away from the hottest new management trends. Instead, they shared specific traits that put them and the companies they led on winning trajectories: a laser-sharp focus on per share value as opposed to earnings or sales growth; an exceptional talent for allocating capital and human resources; and the belief that cash flow, not reported earnings, determines a company’s long-term value.

Drawing on years of research and experience, Thorndike tells eye-opening stories, extracting lessons and revealing a compelling alternative model for anyone interested
summary: The talk argues that successful 'outsider' CEOs, such as Jeff Bezos and the Rales brothers, prioritize optimizing for recurring free cash flow per share and utilizing internal growth as a primary capital allocation channel. The speaker highlights that this approach has proven effective for companies like American Tower, Crown Castle, and Google, often resulting in high internal rates of return (IRR) even when acquisitions appear to defy normal financial metrics. Additionally, the discussion identifies a group of 'mini Berkshire' insurance companies and other firms that embody these outsider principles of disciplined capital allocation and margin expansion.

claims.claim: The speaker notes American Tower has been a great stock over a long period, though its capital allocation approach differs from Crown Castle.
claims.quote: Both have been great, great stocks over a long period of time. But their approaches to capital allocation and to running their businesses are very different.
claims.speaker: William Thorndike

claims.claim: Crown Castle evolved to optimize for recurring free cash flow per share, a metric differentiated from industry peers.
claims.quote: And evolved over time, but eventually, they would just say, we're running our business to optimize for one thing and that's recurring free cash flow per share.
claims.speaker: William Thorndike

claims.claim: Jeff Bezos is identified as a top choice for an outsider CEO among technology CEOs in the last 25 years.
claims.quote: And I can't say that I've studied the company in great detail, but I have read annual reports. And I believe he's optimizing for per share values 5 to 10 years out.
claims.speaker: William Thorndike

claims.claim: The Rales brothers at Danaher are cited as a definite fit for the outsider CEO model.
claims.quote: So you mentioned the Rales brothers at Danaher and Colfax. I think they very definitely fit the model.
claims.speaker: William Thorndike

claims.claim: Mark Leonard runs Constellation Software using many of the outsider principles discussed.
claims.quote: There is a CEO name Mark Leonard who runs a very interesting software business in Canada called Constellation Software using many of these principles.
claims.speaker: William Thorndike

claims.claim: Mike Pearson at Valeant is considered an interesting case to watch, though the speaker notes it is controversial and early days.
claims.quote: I believe, controversial as it is at the moment, that Mike Pearson at Valeant, although it's still early days, has many of these traits.
claims.speaker: William Thorndike

claims.claim: The speaker believes Oracle has been effective in acquisitions, noting it has been a very accretive activity for shareholders over a long period.
claims.quote: I know that Oracle has been acquisitive over a long period of time. And I believe, although I haven't studied the data, that that's been a very accretive activity for shareholders.
claims.speaker: William Thorndike

claims.claim: The speaker notes Facebook has used internal growth as its primary capital allocation channel, describing it as a prudent thing to do.
claims.quote: Facebook, it's extraordinary what's gone on in that business. And their primary capital allocation channel has been internal growth. They've been funding internal growth. That's a very prudent thing to do.
claims.speaker: William Thorndike

claims.claim: The speaker states that funding internal growth has been true for Google and argues it has been a great high IRR activity.
claims.quote: That's been true for Google. Impossible to argue that that hasn't been a great high IRR activity for-- but at some point, the growth levels out.
claims.speaker: William Thorndike

claims.claim: The speaker describes the YouTube acquisition as a phenomenal acquisition that was possible to justify.
claims.quote: When you guys did the YouTube acquisition, by the way, it was also a possible to justify it. That's been a phenomenal acquisition.
claims.speaker: William Thorndike

claims.claim: The speaker finds the WhatsApp acquisition insane on normal financial metrics but believes normal metrics don't necessarily apply and the IRR will be interesting in three years.
claims.quote: I mean, that seems completely insane to me on normal financial metrics, but I don't think normal financial metrics necessarily apply. But we'll be able to calculate the IRR on that three years from now.
claims.speaker: William Thorndike

claims.claim: The speaker finds 3G Capital fascinating and notes they have proven the ability to grow cash flow and increase margins through zero based budgeting.
claims.quote: 3G is just fascinating. It's just fascinating to see what they're doing across these industries. And I don't know-- I'm curious to see what that's going to look like five years from now, but have proven, across a range of businesses now, the ability to grow cash flow, increase margins through zero based budgeting, reducing costs without material declines in revenues.
claims.speaker: William Thorndike
